---

->QUESTION CXII<-

ON BOASTING. — Divided into two articles.

Next, we must consider boasting and irony, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher, in 4 *Ethics*, ch. 7.
First, regarding boasting, two points are inquired into: 1. To which virtue is it opposed; 2. Whether it is a mortal sin.

->ARTICLE FIRST<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, it is proceeded as follows. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes boasting can exist even without a lie; such as when someone shows off their own excellence: for it is said in Esther 1:3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast... that he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom* <note>original: "Divitias gloriæ regni sui"</note> and the greatness and excellence of his power. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is placed by Gregory, 23 *Morals*, ch. 4, from the beginning, as one of the four species of pride, namely when someone boasts of having what they do not have; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that his virtue is not according to it.* And in 31 *Morals*, ch. 7, near the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from vainglory. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

<margin>ART. I. — Boasting, strictly speaking, is a vice whereby someone outwardly exalts oneself above that which is in oneself. Although boasting, according to the use of the word, may also be spoken of regarding the display of truth beyond the opinion or knowledge of others—as it is a vice from its own genus (for thus it is only strictly taken)—it is not spoken of except as the opposite of truth, by way of excess; since only then is it the name of a vice from its own genus. For the display of truth beyond the knowledge of others is not evil from its own genus, but is sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes evil, on account of an evil end (Cajetan).</margin>

<column-break/>

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by wealth; hence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of wealth seems to pertain to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— But on the contrary, there is what the Philosopher says in 2 and 4 *Ethics*, ch. 7, in both places that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that boasting, strictly speaking, seems to imply that a man exalts himself by words. For those things that a man wishes to boast about far and wide, he elevates on high. Now, someone properly exalts oneself when they say something about themselves that is above themselves. This occurs in two ways: sometimes someone speaks of themselves not indeed above that which is in them, but above that which men opine of them; which the Apostle, avoiding, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or heareth anything of me.* — In another way, someone exalts oneself by words, speaking of oneself above that which is in oneself according to the truth of the matter. And because one is more to be judged according to what is in oneself than according to what is in the opinion of others, it is that it is more properly called boasting when someone exalts oneself above what is in oneself than when one exalts oneself above what is in the opinion of others; although in both ways it can be called boasting. And therefore **boasting, strictly speaking, is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds concerning boasting as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way, according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body [of the article], and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way, according to its cause, from which, although not always, yet more frequently it happens, and thus it indeed proceeds from pride as from an interior motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is elevated interiorly through arrogance above themselves, it follows for the most part that they outwardly boast of certain greater things about themselves, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and takes pleasure in this, because such is their habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is exalted above themselves, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is, for the most part, its cause. And for this reason, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. A boaster tends for the most part toward the end of obtaining glory through their boasting; and therefore, according to Gregory, it arises from vainglory according to the nature of the end.

<summary>This page discusses the definition and moral classification of boasting, distinguishing it as a vice of excess that is formally opposed to the virtue of truth, while noting its causal relationship to pride and vainglory.</summary>
